Figure 3: Zeroth Betti numbers (β0) across layers for two eight-layer ReLU architectures. Each plot shows the mean β0 at each layer, its ±1 SD band, and individual seeds. The monotonic decline in the alternating-width model (right) suggests genuine topological simplification rather than simple geometric compression and re-expansion between layers.
Figure 4: Model size versus simplification timing (COM(β0)) on the synthetic dataset, shown separately for each activation function.

Figure 5: Graphical relationship and correlation between early topological simplification (COM(β0)) and reconstruction error (MRD) in architectures trained on the synthetic dataset. The strong negative correlation highlights a clear association between earlier topological simplification and weaker reconstruction performance.

Figure 6: Violin plots of COM(β0 + β1) for three MNIST architectures (tanh activation), ordered left to right by decreasing total hidden-layer width, computed from 30 independently trained networks per configuration. Lower COM indicates earlier topological simplification. For meaning of architecture names, refer to Table B.2. Model sizes are 4096, 1920, and 1440, respectively.

Figure A.1: Reconstructed inputs from two PCNs (red), overlaid on the true manifold Ma (green). Reconstructions by 30x8 leaky (left) remain localized within components, while those by 30x4 10x4 relu (right) are substantially more scattered and disconnected, indicating weaker approximate invertibility, aligning with the former’s significantly lower MRD (0.024 vs. 0.122, respectively).
Table B.1: Summary of architectures trained on the synthetic dataset with their hidden layer widths and activation functions used.

Figure D.1: Bootstrap distributions of COM mean differences between matched PCNs and MLPs. Each panel shows ∆COM = COMPCN −COMMLP for one architecture– activation pair. The dashed vertical line marks zero; all distributions lie to the right of zero, indicating larger COM for PCNs.
